name: Bisabolol

card.summary: A chamomile-derived oil used in skincare as a soothing, calming ingredient to leave irritated skin looking and feeling more comfortable.

quick.overview:
Bisabolol is a fragrant oil from German chamomile, also made synthetically, that appears in moisturisers, sunscreens, aftershaves and soothing serums. Brands use it to make skin look calmer and less red, particularly in formulas for sensitive skin.

It is described as anti-irritant, anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial, and as a penetration enhancer that can help other ingredients absorb. Laboratory and animal work supports several of these properties, while human trials are small and mixed.
quick.how: It is used as an ingredient in cosmetics rather than alone, often in creams, lotions and after-sun or post-treatment products at low concentrations. People pick products labelled "bisabolol" or "chamomile" for sensitive or irritated skin.
quick.risks: Bisabolol is generally well tolerated in cosmetics, though allergy to chamomile-family plants and rare contact reactions are reported. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review has published a safety assessment.

lead: Bisabolol, also called levomenol, is a natural sesquiterpene alcohol and the main constituent of German chamomile (Matricaria recutita) essential oil; the common form is alpha-(-)-bisabolol [1]. It is a colourless viscous oil with a weak sweet floral scent used in fragrance [1].

In skincare it is used for its soothing reputation. Wikipedia describes cosmetic use for centuries, with claims of reducing roughness and repairing sun-damaged skin, along with anti-irritant, anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties and a role as a penetration enhancer that increases absorption of other substances [1]. Looks-wise, it is used to calm redness and irritation from active products such as retinoids, and a recent combination with tretinoin is sold as an acne gel [1].

Human research includes small randomised trials: two that tested bisabolol alongside nifedipine, canola oil and glycerol against experimental irritation [2][3], a trial of its skin-whitening effect in Asian women [4], and a mouthwash trial in maxillofacial surgery [5]. A 2017 safety review appeared in the International Journal of Toxicology [6].

angle.text: Bisabolol is part of "soothing" formulas for sensitive skin and post-treatment care. It is typically a supporting ingredient rather than the main active.

infobox: German chamomile (Matricaria recutita) oil; also synthetic [1]

paras: Cosmetic and pharmaceutical products use bisabolol as a soothing agent and as a penetration enhancer [1]. A review of chamomile describes its traditional uses and the pharmacology of its constituents [7].

Bisabolol is a monocyclic sesquiterpene alcohol with formula C15H26O and molar mass about 222 g/mol. It is poorly soluble in water and soluble in ethanol; synthetic material is usually a racemic mixture, while the natural (-) enantiomer is common in chamomile [1]. Cannabis cultivars with high bisabolol levels also exist [1].

In two randomised trials of anti-irritants in healthy volunteers, researchers induced irritation with sodium lauryl sulfate and nonanoic acid and then applied formulations with nifedipine, (-)-alpha-bisabolol, canola oil or glycerol. In the dose-response trial, only glycerol showed effects better than no treatment; the other three agents, including bisabolol, did not differ significantly [2]. A companion trial examined cumulative irritation [3].

A randomised trial examined the whitening effect of alpha-bisabolol in Asian women [4], and a triple-blind randomised trial assessed alpha-bisabolol mouthwashes for complications after maxillofacial surgery [5]. A 2025 clinical study tested a sunscreen containing nanoencapsulated antioxidants with UV and blue-light protection [8].
A 2017 safety review in the International Journal of Toxicology and a 2010 dermatitis journal entry address bisabolol [6][9].
